questions.question: Explain why an unbalanced equation 'lies', and which law balancing restores.
questions.expected_answer: An unbalanced equation shows different atom counts on each side, implying atoms were created or destroyed. The law of conservation of mass says atoms are only rearranged in reactions, so balancing adjusts the coefficients until every element's count matches across the arrow, making the equation a true statement.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a coefficient and a subscript, and why only one of them may be changed during balancing.
questions.expected_answer: A subscript defines a substance's identity (H2O is water; H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide) and is fixed once the formula is written. A coefficient multiplies the whole formula, changing the amount without altering the identity. Balancing adjusts amounts, not identities, so only coefficients may change.

questions.question: In your own words, justify the carbon-hydrogen-oxygen balancing order for combustion, and describe the audit that ends every balancing exercise.
questions.expected_answer: Carbon and hydrogen each appear in only one product, so their coefficients settle immediately; oxygen appears in both products and alone as O2, so it depends on the others and is balanced last with one clean coefficient. The audit counts every element on both sides (C 3=3, H 8=8, O 10=10 for propane) to prove conservation of mass rather than assume it.
